cases.reason: Gives n*x^(n-1).
cases.answer: If f(x) = x^n, then f'(x) = n · x^(n-1) [2]

cases.reason: Gives the composition chain rule.
Gives ln|x| plus C.
cases.answer: ∫ 1/x dx = ln|x| + C [1]

cases.reason: Gives the power antiderivative and n != -1 condition.
Gives an ordered n-tuple.
cases.answer: A vector v in n-dimensional space is an ordered n-tuple of numbers: v = (v₁, v₂, ..., vₙ) [1]

cases.reason: Gives the sum of component products.
cases.answer: u · v = Σ uᵢ · vᵢ [1]

cases.reason: Gives m by p.
Solves det(A-lambda*I)=0.
cases.answer: Solve det(A - λI) = 0 (characteristic polynomial) [3]

cases.reason: Gives integer currency representation.
cases.answer: Use Integers as currency to eliminate floating-point rounding errors [1].

cases.reason: Distinguishes successful empty search (200 and empty list) from missing resource (404).
cases.answer: A search that finds nothing (e.g., GET /transactions?date=today) is a success. Return 200 OK with an empty list []. A request for a specific entity that is missing (e.g., GET /transactions/tx-123) must return 404 Not Found [1].

cases.reason: Gives 202 Accepted and a Location polling endpoint.
cases.answer: Return 202 Accepted with a Location header pointing to a status polling endpoint, or use Webhooks [1].

cases.reason: Reuses an in-flight result rather than opening a second identical upstream call.
cases.answer: Use request coalescing to deduplicate concurrent identical requests to the same upstream [1]. When a request arrives for key X, check if an upstream call for X is already in-flight. If yes, subscribe the caller to the existing result instead of opening a new connection [1].

cases.reason: Names money, contracts, reputation and law from the institutions table.
cases.answer: Money, contracts, reputation, law [2]

cases.reason: Compares revenue and competition instead of the requested own-app versus embedded delivery distinction.
cases.answer: Embedded fintech combines subscriptions with a share of fees from payment gateways, loan origination, or credit processing [2]. Standalone neobanks such as N26, Chime, Varo, and Monzo compete through their brands, user experience, and additional services [1].

cases.reason: Combines subscriptions and transaction/processing fee volume.
cases.answer: Embedded fintech providers can combine subscriptions with a share of fees from payment gateways, loan origination, or credit processing [1].

cases.reason: Names product count, sales channels and monthly orders.
cases.answer: Subscription tiers are set by product count, connected sales channels, and monthly orders [1].

cases.reason: Distinguishes main-thread command execution from optional other threads for I/O/background work.
cases.answer: Redis keeps its active data in memory [1]. Its command execution is mostly single-threaded: the server handles one command at a time on its main execution thread [1]. Network I/O and background work can use other threads, depending on the Redis version and configuration [1].

cases.reason: Gives CRC16(key) mod 16384 and 16,384 slots, with matching evidence.
cases.answer: The formula is slot = CRC16(key) mod 16384 [1, 2]. The total slot count is 16,384 [1, 2].

cases.reason: The main expired-owner warning is supported, but the added same-token/newer-worker condition is not supported by the cited text and muddles the ownership test.
cases.answer: A worker must compare its token before releasing a Redis lock to avoid accidentally deleting a newer worker’s lock [2]. If a worker’s lock has expired or another worker’s lock exists with the same token, the original worker could delete the marker intended for a different worker, leading to duplicate work [2].

cases.reason: Distinguishes Redis atomic execution from a cross-service SQL transaction.
cases.answer: No. Redis scripts provide atomic execution, not general rollback or a transaction with another service [1].

cases.reason: Explains absent deleted rows versus WAL deletion events.
cases.answer: Polling-based CDC misses deleted rows because a deleted row no longer exists to be queried [2]. Log-Based CDC captures hard deletes because the WAL records the deletion event [1].

cases.reason: Names the durable connect-offsets Kafka topic.
cases.answer: It saves its state in a dedicated, durable Kafka topic called connect-offsets [1].

cases.reason: Provides an idempotent/LSN comparison action for duplicates.
cases.answer: A consumer compares incoming LSNs: if incoming\_lsn <= last\_processed\_lsn, discard it as a duplicate [2].

cases.reason: Uses order_id as partition key and explains per-partition ordering.
cases.answer: CDC engines map the database Primary Key as the partition key in Kafka (partition_key = order_id). Because Kafka guarantees ordering within a single partition, all updates for a specific order land on the same partition and are processed strictly in order [1].

cases.reason: Redirects incoming and outgoing edges to the master entity.
cases.answer: All incoming and outgoing edges redirect to this single master node [3].

cases.reason: Identifies loss of counterfactual reasoning with untyped generic relations.
cases.answer: Generic RELATED_TO or MENTIONS edges weaken a knowledge graph because 90% of edges of this type lose its reasoning power [1, 2]. You cannot run “what-if” counterfactual simulations on an edge that doesn’t specify the nature of the relationship [1, 2].

cases.reason: Separately names structural/ownership and causal/dynamic predicates with examples.
cases.answer: Structural/Ownership: SUBSIDIARY_OF, INVESTED_IN, EMPLOYED_BY [1] and Causal/Dynamic: TRIGGERED, SUPPRESSED, ACCELERATED [1]

cases.reason: Retains distinct authority and provenance rather than weighting a tweet and filing equally.
cases.answer: Not all extracted statements carry equal factual or causal weight. An unverified tweet and an official SEC filing should not create edges with identical authority [1].

cases.reason: Names shared code/heap/globals and private stacks.
cases.answer: The code, global / static variables, and heap are shared by all threads within a process [1, 2]. Each thread has its own private stack [1, 2].

cases.reason: Allows identical virtual addresses backed by different physical memory.
cases.answer: Yes, different processes can use the same virtual address without referring to the same physical address [1].

cases.reason: Lists several supported metadata fields besides file contents.
warnings: Does not list file type; the question asks for metadata examples rather than every field.
cases.answer: File metadata can include: File size, Owner, Permissions, Timestamps, Locations of data blocks [1].

cases.reason: Explains indirect cache/TLB/pipeline warm-up costs.
cases.answer: Context-switch cost can become more expensive indirectly because caches, TLBs, and CPU pipelines may need to warm up again [1].

cases.reason: Gives the exchanges, queues, bindings recovery order.
cases.answer: exchanges first, then queues, then bindings [1].

cases.reason: Contrasts immediate automatic delivery with explicit post-success manual acknowledgement and scopes the loss warning.
cases.answer: Auto acknowledgement (autoAck: true) considers a message delivered as soon as it sends it over the socket [1]. Messages can be lost if the consumer crashes before processing. Manual acknowledgement (autoAck: false) requires the application to explicitly call channel.ack(deliveryTag) after successful processing [2].

cases.reason: Explains TTL and dead-letter routing back to the primary exchange.
cases.answer: The retry queue has x-message-ttl and x-dead-letter-exchange pointing back to the primary exchange, creating a delayed requeue cycle [1].

cases.reason: Directs exhausted retries to a parking lot for inspection.
cases.answer: After all retries are exhausted (e.g., a x-death header shows the message has been retried N times), the message is moved to a parking lot queue for manual inspection [1, 4].

cases.reason: Limits queue/concurrent work when production outpaces consumption; the cited checklist supports the action.
cases.answer: Backpressure: limit queues and concurrent work when producers are faster than consumers [2].

cases.reason: Lists traffic, payload, storage, concurrency and retention inputs.
warnings: Additional OS citations do not support workload estimation; the checklist citation supports the complete answer.
cases.answer: average and peak requests per second, object size, storage growth, read and write volume, bandwidth, concurrent users, and retention time [1, 2].

cases.reason: Asks what temporary state may be lost and how durable fallback/rebuilding works.
cases.answer: Temporary state and recovery: decide what may be lost from memory and how a node, database, or cache outage rebuilds state or falls back to durable storage [1].

cases.reason: Lists compute, memory, storage, bandwidth, operations and third-party usage.
cases.answer: Compute, memory, storage, bandwidth, operations, or third-party usage [1].

cases.reason: Maps the rider to an S2 cell and queries its eight neighbors.
cases.answer: The backend maps a rider’s coordinate to an S2 Cell ID, then queries that cell and its eight neighbors instead of the whole database [3].

cases.reason: Indicates ETA service ranking; the cited section states it ranks returned drive times.
warnings: The ETA-ranking fragment is terse and would be clearer as an explicit sentence selecting ETA over geometric distance.
cases.answer: DISCO → ETA: rank candidates [1]

cases.reason: Distinguishes availability-oriented locations from consistency-oriented matching.
cases.answer: The platform uses different CAP trade-offs for different sub-domains: the Location Tracking Engine uses AP Eventual Consistency [3], while the Matching & Trip State Engine uses CP Strong Consistency [3]. This choice is driven by the requirements of each engine, with location tracking prioritizing high availability and sub-second latency, and matching prioritizing zero double-bookings and financial integrity.

cases.reason: Names all five DOMA layers.
cases.answer: Edge Layer, Presentation Layer, Product Layer, Business Layer, Infrastructure Layer [1]

cases.reason: Names supported parallel audio/caption/frame workflows besides video encoding.
warnings: Omits some source examples; the actual question does not demand an exhaustive list of DAG workflows.
cases.answer: The conceptual video ingestion DAG processes video chunks into 1080p/720p/360p resolutions, extract audio, generate speech-to-text captions, and sample frames [1, 3].

cases.reason: Names .mpd/MPEG-DASH and .m3u8/HLS.
cases.answer: .mpd for MPEG-DASH or .m3u8 for HLS [2]

cases.reason: Distinguishes continuous real-time encoding from uploaded-file batch processing.
cases.answer: Live streaming cannot use the standard VOD DAG because encoding must happen in real time [3]. The live transcoder keeps a small frame buffer, encodes frames on the fly, and sends them to the distribution network [1].

cases.reason: Locates all three requested tiers: edge SSD, regional caches, central blob storage.
cases.answer: Hot content is cached on NVMe/SSD edge servers near the user [1]. Warm content is kept in regional Google data-center caches [1]. Cold content is read from central blob storage over Google’s backbone [1].
